input: When a pure component is held at its boiling point, its liquid and vapour phases are able to coexist alongside one another in a state of phase equilibrium. The condition that has to be satisfied for this equilibrium to hold is that the chemical potential of the component is exactly the same in the liquid phase as it is in the vapour phase. In other words, the component has no tendency to move preferentially in either direction between the two phases, and although individual molecules are constantly passing back and forth across the interface, there is no net transfer of material from one phase to the other. This is an important idea because it explains why boiling takes place at a constant temperature: as long as both phases are present together, any heat that is added to the system is used to convert liquid into vapour rather than to raise the temperature, and the temperature stays fixed at the boiling point for the pressure that has been imposed. The boiling point itself is therefore not an arbitrary property of the component, but the temperature at which the equilibrium between the two phases is established at that pressure. If the temperature were raised above the boiling point at the same pressure, the equality of chemical potential could no longer be maintained with both phases present, and the liquid would disappear entirely, leaving only the vapour as the stable phase.
target: A pure component at its boiling point holds its liquid and vapour phases in equilibrium with each other. The equilibrium condition is stated in words as an equality: the chemical potential of the component in the liquid phase equals the chemical potential of the component in the vapour phase. Chemical potential is the quantity whose equality across a phase boundary marks the absence of any net driving force for transfer, so under the stated condition the component passes between the phases in both directions at equal rates and neither phase grows at the expense of the other. Boiling is the visible form of the condition. Heat added to the mixture at fixed pressure converts liquid into vapour while both phases remain present, and the temperature stays at the boiling point during the conversion because the added heat is taken up by the change of phase rather than by a rise in temperature. The boiling point is in this way fixed by the pressure: for a pure component, each pressure carries the one temperature at which the equality holds with both phases present. A temperature above the boiling point at the same pressure leaves the vapour as the only stable phase, and a temperature below it leaves the liquid; coexistence belongs to the boiling point alone. The condition is stated for a pure component, whose single chemical potential in each phase is enough to fix the equilibrium.
